extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying infringement law
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether conduct or an accused device/process/article falls within a patentee's exclusive rights (making, using, vending) — focusing on machines, manufactures/compositions, and arts, and on doctrines like substantial identity and mechanical equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protects the thing patented, not the product made by it
rubrics_metrics.description: The law protects the thing patented (e.g., the instruments/machine), and not necessarily the product manufactured by it; the exclusive right is to make and use the patented instruments, not to prohibit third parties from selling the articles once sold and mingled with the common mass of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a patented mill/oven gives rights to construct and use the mill/stove, but a purchaser of flour or bread made at that mill/stove is not necessarily an infringer; a vendor who merely buys and sells the product has the right to sell unless he is connected with the use or construction of the patented machine. See discussion and cases (e.g., Kepplinger v. De Young; Simpson v. Wilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor liability where connected with use of patented machine
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person who sells the products is connected with the use or construction of the patented machine, he is responsible as for an infringement and, if the court has jurisdiction of his person, may be enjoined despite use beyond the court's territorial jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the machine is used outside the court's territorial limits, a vendor connected to that use may be restrained. Allegations that the defendant constructed/used the machine in connection with another who did so can make the defendant responsible and subject to injunction and damages; the extent of liability may be regulated by amount of sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial assignment and right to vend manufactured articles outside territory
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of an exclusive right to use a machine and to vend it to others within a specified territory authorizes the assignee to vend elsewhere, out of that territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has so decided; an assignee's territorial rights do not necessarily bar vending articles made by the machine outside the assigned territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: A patent for a manufacture or composition is infringed by making, using, or selling the thing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter is the vendible, tangible product (a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter'), a patent will be infringed by making, using, or selling the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly speaking, any use or consumption of the patented thing could be an infringement, but courts balance this against public convenience; whether an innocent purchaser who consumes a patented medicine is liable is debatable. For perishable/consumable articles, selling or giving them to others to be consumed may be regarded as a violation, because both acts 'make use' of the invention to the injury of the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a patented machine is altogether prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject of the patent is a machine, the statute vests in the patentee the exclusive right to use the machine; the 'using' of the machine is altogether prohibited to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee's rights include both making the machine and producing the effect/result intended by it. Even executing an order to manufacture a patented article (on a model) can constitute infringement, regardless of the manufacturer's initial knowledge of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: A patent for an art (process) is infringed by practising the same art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an art (process/method) is the subject-matter of a patent, the patent will be infringed by exercising or practising the same art — which will constitute a 'using' of the invention or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering or executing production by the same process, even via agents or third parties, can satisfy this criterion (see cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement requires substantial identity (same principle or modus operandi)
rubrics_metrics.description: The central question in infringement is whether the accused thing is the same as the patented one — i.e., whether there is substantial identity described by terms like 'same principle', 'same modus operandi', or a copy with only variations consistent with being in substance the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What amounts to 'substantial identity' cannot be stated in general terms and depends on the circumstances and reported cases. Judges have used tests like 'same principle' but caution that 'principle' must be understood in a legal sense (peculiar structure/constituent parts or modus operandi), not as elementary natural principles. The safest guide is to ask what result is obtained and what is essential to that object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine principle by result and essential elements, not mere form
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the 'principle' of an invention, identify the result to be obtained and whatever is essential to that object, independent of mere form and proportions; such essentials may be considered the principle of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different minds may disagree about what is essential, so expert evidence and careful factual analysis are often necessary. The legal meaning of 'principle' (with respect to machines) is the peculiar structure or constituent parts and their mode of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine infringes if it incorporates the substance of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine infringes if it incorporates in its structure and operation the substance of the patented invention — i.e., by an arrangement of mechanism that performs the same service or produces the same effect in the same, or substantially the same, way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations (Wyeth v. Stone): even if an accused machine differs in certain elements (single vs double series of cutters), if it is substantially the same in mode of operation and copies the substance of the invention, it is infringement. The question is factual and depends on inspection and expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration defeats infringement; mere form differences do not
rubrics_metrics.description: If differences between two machines are not mere differences of form but are material alterations of structure or operation (substantially different combinations of mechanism to effect the purpose), they will not be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an alteration is material is generally a question of fact for the jury. Examples: differences in valve shapes or arrangements may be material; changes that preserve the same mode of operation are likely immaterial. The court must examine whether the accused device produces the given effect by substantially the same mode of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of mechanical equivalents (identity of purpose over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention is not for a combination, the absence of two or three things mentioned in the specification will not prevent recovery if the principle is applied in the same way — i.e., mechanical equivalents may constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical equivalents focus on identity of purpose, not form or name; whether something is a mechanical equivalent is a question of fact for the jury, based on expert testimony and inspection. Two things may be equivalents in some circumstances and not in others; mere colorable alterations intended to evade the patent may be disregarded. Names and labels are of comparative little importance — the test is whether the defendant accomplishes the same purpose, object, or effect as the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of agents/contractors executing orders to make patented articles
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who executes an order to manufacture a patented article (on a model) for another may be guilty of infringement, even if at the time of beginning he had no knowledge of the plaintiff's patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act of making under contract or by agency can be treated as making/using the patented invention. Conversely, questions remain about the liability of a mere agent or purchaser acting for another; jurisdictional and fact-specific issues determine reach of liability.
